title: OpenAI agents linked to previously undisclosed cyberattack on RubyGems - WSJ
full_text:
U.S. stocks slip for the week on soaring oil, sharp surge in Fed rate hike bets
Investing.com -- OpenAI agents were involved in a previously undisclosed May cyberattack that overwhelmed the RubyGems software service, the Wall Street Journal reported exclusively on Friday.
OpenAI confirmed its agents were involved after a group of AI researchers linked them to the incident. The company said the agents had used RubyGems to access the internet for benign tasks and retrieve publicly available information during training.
The incident occurred two months before a separate episode involving OpenAI agents and AI platform Hugging Face. In that case, as many as 1,200 agents coordinated using a makeshift message board they created without the company’s knowledge.
The May attack, dubbed "GemStuffer" by security researchers, began when agents started creating RubyGems accounts every two to three minutes and uploading hundreds of files containing webpages scraped from the internet.
The activity became large enough that RubyGems, a widely used service for distributing software packages to developers, suspended new account registrations for four days.
Researchers said the agents also tried to exploit two vulnerabilities that could have let them publish new versions of other users’ software packages. One was described as a previously unknown zero-day vulnerability, though OpenAI said it could not verify that finding.
Ruby Central, the nonprofit operating RubyGems, said the incident represented a major attack by volume but did not appear to have successfully exploited the alleged zero-day flaw.
The episode adds to scrutiny of rapidly improving AI agents and their cybersecurity capabilities. Researchers have documented instances involving systems from several AI developers taking actions their operators did not intend.
OpenAI has acknowledged the broader concern, calling for better industry standards for reporting "misalignment incidents" in which agents behave beyond their intended parameters.
The RubyGems case suggests those concerns are moving beyond controlled experiments. The incident caused relatively limited damage, but autonomous agents generated enough real-world activity to disrupt a major software service for several days.

title: Trump says he’s open to Chinese automakers building cars in the U.S.
full_text:
U.S. stocks slip for the week on soaring oil, sharp surge in Fed rate hike bets
Investing.com -- President Donald Trump said he would be open to Chinese automakers building vehicles in the United States with American workers, even as he pledged to maintain restrictions that have effectively shut Chinese-made cars out of the U.S. market.
Trump rejected reports that he could allow vehicles built in China to be imported into the U.S., saying the domestic market could be "overrun" if existing restrictions were lifted.
He drew a distinction between imports and Chinese companies manufacturing vehicles inside the U.S., comparing such investment with production by Japanese automakers.
"If China wanted to come in, and open a plant to build their cars here, I’d be okay with it," Trump said in a Fox News interview, adding that Chinese manufacturers would need to hire American workers.
Chinese electric-vehicle makers including BYD and Geely Automobile have expanded rapidly overseas, raising concerns among U.S. automakers as their vehicles gain ground in markets including Canada and Mexico.
Chinese cars are effectively excluded from the U.S. through steep tariffs and Commerce Department restrictions covering connected-vehicle systems linked to countries including China.
Trump’s comments come ahead of a planned summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington. He made similar remarks in January, when he said Chinese automakers could potentially manufacture vehicles in the U.S.
Ford (NYSE:F) Chief Executive Jim Farley and Trump administration officials also held preliminary discussions earlier this year about a possible framework under which Chinese companies could manufacture cars in the U.S. with protections for domestic automakers. No decisions were reached.
The prospect remains politically contentious. Senators Elissa Slotkin and Bernie Moreno have introduced legislation aimed at restricting connected vehicles, software and hardware linked to China and other countries considered U.S. adversaries.
The measure, backed by Ford, General Motors (NYSE:GM) and the United Auto Workers, would also prohibit sales of connected vehicles from automakers more than 15% owned by Chinese entities.

title: How much more gold could central banks buy?
full_text:
U.S. stocks slip for the week on soaring oil, sharp surge in Fed rate hike bets
Investing.com -- Central banks could have substantial room to keep buying gold after purchases surged in recent years, with BofA estimating that under-allocated institutions may need more than 20,000 tonnes to reach what it views as an efficient reserve allocation.
Central-bank buying has been a major feature of the gold market since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. BofA said purchases have helped drive the three-year bull market in bullion, with annual buying recently exceeding 1,000 tonnes.
The firm uses a framework under which gold accounts for 30% of total reserve assets, the level at which its commodities team estimates the information ratio of an average central-bank portfolio is maximized.
On a global basis, central banks would need to purchase just under 2,300 tonnes to reach that threshold, equivalent to roughly two years of buying at recent rates.
The potential is much larger when central banks already holding at least 30% of reserves in gold are excluded. BofA estimates the remaining institutions would need to acquire about 20,333 tonnes to reach the target, representing more than two decades of purchases at the recent pace.
China has the largest potential shortfall among individual central banks below the threshold. BofA estimates China would need another 5,628 tonnes, compared with 1,866 tonnes for Japan and 1,192 tonnes for Switzerland. Taiwan, South Korea, Saudi Arabia and Singapore would each require more than 700 tonnes.
The World Gold Council’s latest data put official global gold holdings at about 36,705 tonnes. Central-bank net purchases reached a record 1,092 tonnes in 2024.
Türkiye has been the biggest buyer since March 2022, accumulating 815 tonnes, closely followed by Poland at 808 tonnes. Selling has been considerably smaller, led by Sri Lanka at 387 tonnes and Suriname at 265 tonnes.
BofA sees the gap between current and potential allocations as supportive for gold, particularly if reserve diversification continues and under-allocated central banks gradually increase their exposure.

title: U.S. links Chinese satellite imagery to deadly Iranian strike - WSJ
full_text:
U.S. stocks slip for the week on soaring oil, sharp surge in Fed rate hike bets
Investing.com -- U.S. officials have linked high-resolution satellite imagery supplied to Iran by Chinese entities to a July missile strike on a U.S. base in Jordan that killed three American troops, the Wall Street Journal reported exclusively on Friday.
The officials did not identify the Chinese entities that provided the imagery and did not allege direct involvement by Beijing. Iran obtained images both before and after the July 17 attack on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, according to the report.
Iranian ballistic missiles struck a housing area where U.S. troops were sleeping, killing three soldiers and wounding four others. The attack was one of three missile strikes against the base within 24 hours and marked the first U.S. deaths since an April ceasefire.
U.S. officials raised the satellite imagery with Chinese counterparts, who challenged the findings and requested evidence. China’s embassy in Washington did not address the specific allegations but said the country’s cooperation with Iran complied with international law.
The findings could add friction to U.S.-China relations ahead of a planned Sept. 24 summit between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Washington had warned Beijing for months that Chinese companies were providing satellite imagery that Iran could use to target U.S. forces. The Trump administration sanctioned Chinese companies MizarVision, Earth Eye and Chang Guang in May over such concerns.
Officials said Iranian targeting appeared to improve over the summer after earlier U.S. attacks had degraded Tehran’s ability to track battlefield developments. High-resolution satellite images could help identify recent changes at military installations and assess damage after strikes.
U.S. officials are also examining whether Chinese assistance could be helping Iran track American naval assets. Iran has recently fired ballistic missiles at a U.S. aircraft carrier and other warships, with officials saying its ability to target moving vessels appeared to be improving.
Iran also receives intelligence and imagery from its own satellites, human sources and Russia, meaning the Chinese imagery was likely one of several sources used for targeting.

title: UBS sees Chinese carmakers reach 37% globally by 2030
full_text:
U.S. stocks slip for the week on soaring oil, sharp surge in Fed rate hike bets
Investing.com -- Chinese automakers are set to capture 37% of the global car market by 2030, up from 22% in the first half of 2026, as stronger consumer acceptance supports their expansion beyond China, UBS analysts said.
The forecast was raised from 35%, with the projected share in Europe also increased to 20% from 18%. Chinese brands currently hold about 8% of the European market, with recent gains running faster than previously expected.
A UBS Evidence Lab survey of 12,000 consumers found 36% of European respondents would consider buying an electric vehicle from a Chinese brand. Interest in Chinese brands in Europe has moved above that for Japanese and Korean brands combined.
Value for money remains the biggest attraction, cited by 66% of prospective Chinese EV buyers globally. Advanced technology, including digital features and autonomous-driving capabilities, ranked second at 61%.
Chinese automakers have gained between 9 and 12 percentage points of market share across Europe, Latin America, parts of Asia and the Middle East and Africa since 2019. Weak domestic demand in China has also increased pressure on manufacturers to expand exports.
Europe remains a key battleground. Potential tariffs on plug-in hybrids and new local-content requirements could slow Chinese brands, alongside weaker residual values, limited aftersales networks and difficulties entering the corporate fleet market.
Under the base case, a small group including BYD, Geely, Chery, SAIC, Leapmotor and Xiaomi could emerge as the leading Chinese players overseas. An upside scenario puts their global share as high as 45% and European share at 30% by 2030. A downside scenario sees the figures limited to 33% globally and 15% in Europe.
European and Asian mass-market automakers face the greatest competitive pressure. U.S. manufacturers remain better insulated, with Chinese automakers effectively locked out of the U.S. market by trade barriers. Luxury manufacturers are also expected to prove more resilient than mass-market rivals.

title: Nvidia in talks to invest up to $10 billion in Anthropic IPO - Reuters
full_text:
U.S. stocks slip for the week on soaring oil, sharp surge in Fed rate hike bets
Investing.com -- Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) is in talks to become an anchor investor in Anthropic’s planned initial public offering, potentially committing as much as $10 billion to what could become the largest IPO on record, Reuters reported exclusively on Friday.
Anthropic is seeking to raise as much as $100 billion at a valuation of around $2 trillion, according to people familiar with the discussions. The plans remain under negotiation and could change.
Nvidia’s involvement would deepen its relationship with one of its major AI-chip customers and provide Anthropic with a prominent early backer for the listing. An anchor commitment could also help gauge investor appetite for the high valuations and capital requirements of frontier AI companies.
Anthropic declined to comment, and Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The two companies already have substantial financial and commercial ties. Nvidia said in November 2025 that it would invest up to $10 billion in Anthropic under a broader partnership that included a commitment by the AI startup to purchase $30 billion of Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) Azure computing capacity powered by Nvidia chips.
Anthropic is also backed by Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) and Alphabet’s (NASDAQ:GOOGL) Google, both major suppliers of its computing infrastructure. In April, Anthropic committed more than $100 billion over a decade to Amazon Web Services and plans to use more than one million of Amazon’s Trainium2 chips.
The Claude developer has also agreed with Google and Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) to add multiple gigawatts of TPU capacity as it seeks more computing power to support rapid revenue growth.
Anthropic raised $65 billion in May at a post-money valuation of $965 billion. Its annualized revenue run rate surpassed $65 billion by the end of July, up from roughly $9 billion at the end of 2025.
The IPO is expected to be completed before the U.S. midterm elections in November. U.S. IPOs excluding special-purpose acquisition companies had already raised a record $137 billion through August, according to Dealogic.

title: Trump criticizes Smithsonian’s focus on oppression
full_text:
U.S. stocks slip for the week on soaring oil, sharp surge in Fed rate hike bets
By Kanishka Singh
WASHINGTON, Sept 11 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump criticized what he called the Smithsonian’s overwhelming focus on oppression on Friday and called for a five-year exhibition on George Washington, in his latest critique of an institution he has repeatedly attacked.
The Republican leader has denounced the Smithsonian for months, in what critics call part of a campaign to present U.S. history from a conservative point of view. On Tuesday, Smithsonian chief Lonnie Bunch said he was retiring.
Trump said on Truth Social that "under recently ended leadership," the Smithsonian took steps "to focus attention overwhelmingly on those who have been oppressed, but there is almost no attention paid to those who triumphed over great oppression, and against great odds."
"I am calling on the Smithsonian Institution to honor the Life and Legacy of George Washington, America’s Greatest Hero, with a five-year exhibition at the National Museum of American History, beginning now, and continuing through, February 22, 2032, the 300th anniversary of Washington’s birth," Trump added.
Trump said he was also calling on the Smithsonian to "erect a 30-foot (9-m) ’Colossus statue’" of Washington outside the museum.
He also asked the Smithsonian to install an 11-foot (3.4-m)statue of Washington that was featured at the recent Freedom 250 Grand Prix race in the museum’s Flag Hall.
The Trump administration has previously threatened to cut federal funding and federal agencies’ support for the Smithsonian, with Trump expressing displeasure at what he called the institution’s excessive focus on how bad slavery was.
Last year, his administration launched a review of some museums and his White House has accused the institution’s National Museum of American History of "thinly veiled anti-Americanism."
Trump has also ordered installation of signs outside the museum to reflect his administration’s criticism.
Historians and civil rights advocates have denounced Trump’s attacks and his accusations against the institution, saying such steps risk reversing social progress and undermine the acknowledgement of critical phases of U.S. history.
Trump says he aims to remove "anti-American ideology."
Bunch has said the White House’s accusations against the National Museum of American History were unfair.
The Smithsonian is a vast museum and research complex and a premier exhibition space for U.S. history and culture, with 21 museums and galleries and the National Zoo.
Trump has targeted U.S. cultural and historical institutions - from museums to monuments to national parks - with his declarations and orders leading to the dismantling of slavery exhibits and the restoration of Confederate statues.

title: Saudis shut down oil pipeline as Houthis tighten grip on Red Sea shipping
full_text:
U.S. stocks slip for the week on soaring oil, sharp surge in Fed rate hike bets
By Mohammed Ghobari, Eman Abouhassira and Yasmine Ghania
ADEN/DUBAI, Sept 12 (Reuters) - Saudi Arabia has shut down its East-West pipeline after the vital oil conduit came under aerial attack in the widening Middle East war.
The world’s largest crude oil exporter temporarily closed the pipeline after a drone attack that both Baghdad and Riyadh said had originated in Iraq, where Iranian-backed militias operate. Iraq dismissed a military commander on Saturday in response to the attack.
The 1,200-kilometre (745-mile) pipeline running across the Arabian Peninsula had helped Saudi Arabia to bypass a shipping logjam in the Strait of Hormuz, where tanker traffic has slowed to a trickle due to the war between the U.S. and Iran.
The Saudi energy ministry said it had shut the pipeline as a precaution. The line has been moving 4 million to 5 million barrels per day in recent months, amounting to 4% to 5% of global supply, according to ship tracking companies and analysts.
The attack comes as Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in Yemen tightened their grip in the Red Sea, which combined with the Strait of Hormuz disruptions has put an energy squeeze on both sides of the Arabian Peninsula and sent global oil prices back above $100 per barrel.
Four Yemeni government sources told Reuters that Houthis had seized the strategic island of Perim on Friday at the mouth of the Red Sea, in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The dual attacks reported on Friday - on the pipeline and Perim island - could represent a dangerous escalation while diplomatic efforts to end the war have stalled.
Saudi Arabia has asked Washington for military help with the Houthis, sources said, at a time when higher fuel prices during the war have already exacted a political toll on U.S. President Donald Trump and his Republican Party ahead of November congressional elections.
The East-West pipeline was hit on Thursday morning in Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh and Medina regions, the Saudi energy ministry said.
It was not immediately clear who was responsible for the strikes. Satellite images showed black smoke rising from an area of the pipeline south of Medina. The attack resulted in some injuries and damage that was being assessed, the Saudi foreign ministry said without detailing the impact on exports.
The cashiered Iraqi military commander had led operations in Maysan province, according to Saturday’s statement by the Iraqi prime minister’s office. Maysan province, which borders Iran in southeastern Iraq, has long been regarded as an area where Iran-backed Shi’ite militias operate and maintain influence.
Saudi Arabia has opted against retaliation so far following a request from the Iraqi prime minister, the Saudi foreign ministry said in a statement, while adding the kingdom reserves the right to "take all measures necessary" to protect its interests. Iraq’s government condemned attacks.
Saudi crude supply fell to the lowest levels in more than three decades, the International Energy Agency said on Friday, partly due to attacks on ships transiting Bab el-Mandeb by Houthi-linked groups.
Iraq responded by ordering the closure of the Shalamcheh border crossing between Iraq and Iran as a precautionary measure, two security sources told Reuters. The crossing serves as one of the main routes for imports to Iraq of vegetables and other food supplies from Iran.
The two sources said a widescale operation was under way to find those responsible for the pipeline attack.
COUNTERATTACK PLANNED
If the Houthis gain control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, their backer Iran could gain a critical advantage in its war with the U.S.
Yemeni government forces indicated they would try to retake areas captured by the Houthis — mountain fighters who withstood years of devastating Saudi airstrikes during Yemen’s civil war — in their lightning offensive this week along the Red Sea coastline.
Reuters reported on Thursday that the dramatic Houthi advance down Yemen’s Red Sea coast came with direct guidance from Iran’s Revolutionary Guards.
Iran told the Houthis last week to escalate their attacks on Saudi Arabia and promised more funding, weapons and senior officers to help them do so, two Iranian sources said.
Iran describes the Houthis as an ally but publicly denies giving them military direction, saying they are "not a proxy".
The Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said maritime navigation remained safe for all shipping except Saudi vessels subject to a previously announced ban.
SAUDIS SEEK HELP
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called Trump at least twice on Thursday to request U.S. military help in fighting the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told Reuters on Friday, confirming an earlier report by Axios.
Washington told Riyadh it was not willing to take direct military action for now but would help with intelligence sharing and targeting, the two sources said.
The White House did not address a Reuters question on any phone calls between the two leaders, but a senior administration official speaking on the condition of anonymity said Washington was in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government.

title: Adobe beats Q3 targets, but shares slide on soft Q4 sales guidance
full_text:
U.S. stocks slip for the week on soaring oil, sharp surge in Fed rate hike bets
Investing.com -- Adobe Inc. (NASDAQ:ADBE) topped Wall Street’s third-quarter estimates on robust subscription growth, though shares edged down 2.7% in premarket trading Friday after the software maker delivered a fourth-quarter revenue forecast that fell just short of expectations.
The software company posted adjusted earnings per share of $6.13 for the third quarter, surpassing the analyst consensus of $6.07. Revenue reached $6.76 billion, beating the $6.69 billion estimate and representing 13% growth YoY. For the fourth quarter, Adobe issued revenue guidance of $6.80 billion to $6.85 billion, with a midpoint of $6.825 billion that falls short of the $6.85 billion analyst consensus. The company expects fourth quarter adjusted EPS of $6.30 to $6.35, with a midpoint of $6.325 billion matching the $6.30 consensus.
Adobe raised its full-year fiscal 2026 revenue guidance to a range of $26.576 billion to $26.626 billion and increased its full-year adjusted EPS target to $24.45 to $24.50. The company also announced reaching a milestone of more than one billion monthly active users across its creativity and productivity solutions.
"Results were uneventful with a small revenue beat & raise and unchanged operating margin views," Jefferies analysts commented, adding that the company’s valuation remains "depressed as investors await clarity."
Total Customer Group subscription revenue was $6.56 billion, up 14% YoY. Business Professionals & Consumers subscription revenue grew 16% YoY to $1.91 billion, while Creative & Marketing Professionals subscription revenue increased 13% YoY to $4.65 billion. The company generated $2.52 billion in cash flows from operations during the quarter and repurchased approximately 9.5 million shares. Total annualized recurring revenue exiting the quarter was $27.50 billion.
"Adobe delivered record Q3 results, reflecting the strength of our AI innovation, expanding customer reach and leadership across creativity, productivity and customer experience," said Shantanu Narayen, chair and CEO.
Vahid Karaahmetovic contributed to this report.

title: Australia’s Optus apologises for outage that disrupted emergency calls
full_text:
U.S. stocks slip for the week on soaring oil, sharp surge in Fed rate hike bets
(Corrects grammar and use of partial quote in paragraph 2)
SYDNEY, Sept 12 (Reuters) - Optus, Australia’s No. 2 telecom carrier, on Saturday apologised a day after an outage on its network impacted users across three states and disrupted some emergency services calls.
The 76-minute technical glitch on Friday affected Optus voice calling services in parts of Victoria, South Australia, Tasmania states and the Northern Territory, with some customers experiencing "intermittent call dropouts", Optus said in a statement.
"We sincerely apologise to customers for the disruption," the statement said.
The outage follows an Optus network issue last year that left hundreds of people unable to contact police, fire and ambulance services and resulted in two deaths.
Chris Bowen, a senior minister in the country’s centre-left government, said it was "deeply concerning" that another outage had hit Optus customers.
"All the necessary investigations have begun," Bowen said in televised remarks. "It’s an obligation on our telecommunications companies to keep all their technology for triple-0 calls in the best possible working order."
Police in Victoria said they completed around 40 welfare checks on callers hit by Friday’s outage.
"There were no adverse outcomes or issues of note," a police spokesperson said in a statement.
In 2024, Optus, owned by Singapore Telecommunications, was fined A$12 million by regulators for failing to provide emergency call services to thousands during a nationwide outage in 2023. Optus also suffered a cyberattack in 2022 that affected the data of around 9.5 million Australians.

title: Trump says he would be OK with China building cars in US
full_text:
U.S. stocks slip for the week on soaring oil, sharp surge in Fed rate hike bets
By David Shepardson
WASHINGTON, Sept 11 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Friday he would not oppose Chinese automakers building cars in the United States despite widespread opposition from U.S. lawmakers and car companies.
"If China wanted to come in and open a plant to build their cars here, I’d be okay with that," Trump said in an interview on the Fox News program "The Ingraham Angle."
"Japan does it, but they hire our people. The big thing is they hire our people," he said.
He added that he does not want Chinese automakers to build cars in Mexico and ship them to the United States. "I’m not knocking Chinese cars," Trump said.
U.S. automakers have urged Trump, who is due to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington in two weeks, not to agree to allow Chinese automakers access to the U.S. market.
On Wednesday, U.S. Senator Elissa Slotkin, a Michigan Democrat, said there were "rumors that Trump is planning to allow Chinese cars to be sold in the U.S., as part of a larger deal he’s putting together. That would be a strategic mistake."
Trump called Slotkin’s statement a "total phony rumor" and said he had kept Chinese vehicles out of the United States.
A regulation imposed by former President Joe Biden’s administration in early 2025 effectively bans all Chinese automakers from selling or building passenger vehicles in the U.S. Washington also maintains more than 100% tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles.
Last week, a group representing nearly all major automakers urged Congress to quickly pass legislation permanently barring Chinese vehicles from the U.S. market.
The Alliance for Automotive Innovation, which represents General Motors, Ford, Toyota, Volkswagen, Hyundai, Honda, Stellantis and others, called for passage of the bill by the end of December.
"Right now, Chinese automakers are dumping subsidized vehicles with connected software and hardware around the world," the group’s CEO, John Bozzella, said in a letter to congressional leaders.

title: Houthis seize Red Sea coast as Saudi pipeline shutdown deepens oil risks
full_text:
U.S. stocks slip for the week on soaring oil, sharp surge in Fed rate hike bets
Investing.com -- The Iran war widened its impact on global energy and shipping routes on Saturday as Iran-aligned Houthi forces consolidated control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and Saudi Arabia kept its East-West oil pipeline shut following a drone attack launched from Iraq.
The Houthi advance gives the group control of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline, including positions near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a major shipping route linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden. The group has already threatened commercial traffic in the region for years, but its latest territorial gains strengthen its position along the waterway.
Saudi Arabia suspended its East-West pipeline after several drones struck the system, causing injuries and damage. The pipeline carries crude from eastern Saudi fields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, providing Riyadh with a route that avoids the Strait of Hormuz.
The shutdown comes as traffic through Hormuz remains heavily constrained. The U.S. has reportedly narrowed military-protected sailing periods for tankers to two daily time slots after Iran stepped up attacks on vessels travelling at night.
Iranian officials are expected to meet representatives from Gulf states in Oman on Monday to discuss commercial shipping through Hormuz. Iran and Oman have already discussed a temporary shipping route and short-term demining measures, with Gulf countries expected to take part in talks over maritime security.
Iraq ordered the closure of the Shalamcheh border crossing with Iran after confirming the drones that hit the Saudi pipeline originated from Iraqi territory. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi also ordered an investigation and dismissed a regional military commander.
The energy impact is spreading beyond the Gulf. China raised retail gasoline and diesel prices on Saturday, citing higher international crude prices linked to the U.S.-Iran conflict. A White House economic official also blamed record U.S. diesel prices on disruptions to refined-fuel production in the Middle East and Russia.
The fighting in Yemen is also worsening the humanitarian situation. Around 46,000 people have been displaced since clashes intensified last week, according to the UN migration agency, with hundreds of Yemeni refugees reaching Djibouti.
Diplomatic prospects remain uncertain. A senior Iranian lawmaker said talks with Washington would have no value unless the U.S. accepted Tehran’s conditions, signaling that efforts to reduce tensions remain stalled.

title: Lagarde enters French election debate as ECB exit speculation grows
full_text:
U.S. stocks slip for the week on soaring oil, sharp surge in Fed rate hike bets
Investing.com -- European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde is stepping into France’s presidential election debate with an appearance at a political gathering in Normandy, adding to speculation that she could leave the ECB before her term ends.
Lagarde is due to speak at the Fête de la Pomme, an annual event hosted by Normandy regional president Hervé Morin that has become a gathering place for French political figures and presidential hopefuls.
Her appearance comes days after the ECB delivered a second interest-rate increase aimed at containing inflation pressures linked to the Iran war.
Lagarde has previously described the French presidency as a "terrible job," but she has also said she wants a European voice represented in the election campaign and has declined to rule out leaving the ECB before her mandate expires in October 2027.
Speculation over her future has intensified ahead of the publication of her memoir, "Lady First," in January. The World Economic Forum has also been discussed as a possible destination.
France’s election campaign is gathering pace with less than eight months before the first round. Marine Le Pen currently holds a strong polling lead, with the centrist vote divided among several candidates.
Far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon has also gained attention with proposals to cancel French government bonds held by the ECB and Bank of France. Lagarde said this week that such a move would be legally impossible and financially dangerous.
Centrist politicians are pushing for a primary to narrow the number of moderate candidates, including former prime ministers Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal, amid concerns that a fragmented field could benefit Le Pen and Mélenchon.
Morin, who invited Lagarde to the event, has argued that France and Europe face major economic and political challenges and has criticized proposals to cancel public debt.
Lagarde previously served as France’s finance minister before leaving domestic politics to head the International Monetary Fund. Her appearance in Normandy is likely to fuel further questions over whether she intends to play a larger role in French politics.

title: Ford to recall about 223,500 US vehicles over fuel tank issues
full_text:
Sept 12 (Reuters) - Ford is recalling 223,472 vehicles in the U.S. due to leaky and improperly secured fuel tanks that may detach from the vehicle while driving, the U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said on Saturday.
Here are some more details from the NHTSA advisory:
• A detached tank can create a road hazard, increasing the risk of a crash, while a fuel leak can cause an engine stall or increase the risk of a fire.
• Certain 2023-2027 F-150 vehicles will be recalled due to this concern.
• Dealers will inspect and replace the fuel tank straps, as necessary, free of charge.

title: Meloni sees Italy 2026 growth at 1%, matching euro zone
full_text:
U.S. stocks slip for the week on soaring oil, sharp surge in Fed rate hike bets
MILAN, Sept 12 (Reuters) - Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expects Italy’s economy to grow by 1% this year, in line with the euro zone, she said in an interview with newspaper Il Foglio published on Saturday.
• Meloni’s government in April forecast 2026 gross domestic product growth of 0.6%, but budget watchdog UPB last month issued a more upbeat projection of 0.9%.
• "The Italian economy is holding up well, and data from the first six months of the year could point to 2026 growth of 1%, in line with, if not above, that of the euro zone," Meloni told Il Foglio.
• Italian GDP rose by 0.3% quarter-on-quarter in January to March and by 0.2% in the second quarter.
• So-called "acquired growth" stood at 0.8% at the end of June, meaning that even if GDP is flat in each of the remaining two quarters of 2026, full-year growth will be up 0.8% from 2025.
• "It is also true that the Italian economy has struggled for many years to achieve sustained and steady growth," Meloni added, citing energy costs and low productivity among the reasons.
• "We are working to address these issues, but the results of those efforts will only become visible over the medium term," she said.
• The Italian economy grew 0.5% in 2025.
• It hasn’t exceeded 1% in the last three years despite the steady influx of tens of billions of euros of COVID-19 recovery funds from the European Union.

title: Burnham faces UK economic test as budget day approaches
full_text:
U.S. stocks slip for the week on soaring oil, sharp surge in Fed rate hike bets
Investing.com -- UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham is facing pressure to define his government’s economic strategy ahead of the Oct. 28 budget, with Labour officials questioning how his administration will tackle weaker growth, strained public finances and higher inflation, Bloomberg reported on Saturday.
Burnham has pushed ministers and civil servants to move quickly since replacing Keir Starmer, encouraging his team to overcome bureaucratic and legal obstacles rather than accept that policy changes cannot be delivered.
The approach has produced several early political wins, but officials and Labour figures told Bloomberg the harder economic decisions remain unresolved.
Chancellor John Healey pledged fiscal stability in his first major speech this week and stressed the need to reduce borrowing. His comments caused some confusion, with observers expecting the government to loosen its fiscal rules to permit more borrowing at the October budget.
Burnham has also expressed a preference for cutting rather than raising taxes, even as economists see tax increases as necessary to address a gap in the public finances.
Questions also remain over who is directing economic policy. Healey’s Treasury, Burnham’s new No. 10 North operation in Manchester and officials in Downing Street are all involved in developing growth policies.
Several major spending decisions have been deferred. The government is moving toward raising defense expenditure to 3% of GDP by 2030, but its funding plan is not expected until next year. Burnham also wants to reduce welfare spending, though the scale and timing remain unclear.
Plans to nationalize Thames Water have been delayed amid concerns over the cost, and decisions on further drilling at the Jackdaw and Rosebank oil and gas fields have been pushed later into the autumn.
Labour has strengthened in national polling since Burnham took office, and his allies expect more of the government’s long-term economic direction to emerge in a 10-year plan scheduled for December.
The more immediate challenge comes with the October budget, as officials weigh the impact of the Iran war on inflation and economic growth alongside pressure on government finances.

title: Global funds retreat from Indian stocks as some cut exposure to zero - Bloomberg
full_text:
U.S. stocks slip for the week on soaring oil, sharp surge in Fed rate hike bets
Investing.com -- Global investors are pulling back from Indian equities, with some money managers cutting their allocations to zero as weak earnings, elevated valuations, and the lack of a major artificial-intelligence investment theme reduce the market’s appeal, Bloomberg reported on Saturday.
Foreign portfolio ownership of companies listed on India’s National Stock Exchange has fallen to a 17-year low. Overseas funds have withdrawn a net $25 billion from Indian stocks this year, shifting capital toward markets such as Taiwan and South Korea that offer greater exposure to the AI investment boom.
Reed Capital Partners exited its Indian equity portfolio about a month ago, and money managers at Janus Henderson Investors and Vantage Point Asset Management have also reduced India exposure to zero over roughly the past year.
Indian stocks remain expensive relative to emerging-market peers. The Nifty 50 trades at about 17.6 times forward earnings and commands a 77% valuation premium to the MSCI Emerging Markets Index.
The Nifty is trading near levels last seen in mid-2024 and is on course to end a decade-long run of annual gains. India’s weighting in the MSCI Emerging Markets Index has dropped to about 11% from 16% a year earlier.
Higher oil prices and a weaker rupee have added to investor concerns. India’s reliance on imported energy has increased pressure on its current account during the U.S.-Iran war, with the rupee falling to a record low and ranking among Asia’s weakest currencies this year.
Domestic investors have helped offset foreign selling, purchasing a net $60 billion of stocks this year, according to BSE data.
Some investors remain bullish. Morgan Stanley expects India to benefit from a multi-quarter economic growth upcycle and sees the BSE Sensex rising 19% to 89,000 by June 2027 under its base case. Its bull-case target is 100,000.
